Content:
The cosine function has infinitely many zeros and an infinite number of points where the function reaches its maximum and minimum value. Let's write general expressions for these properties, assuming [MATH: n] is an integer.

Content:
The Zeros of the Function

Content:
From the graph, we see that the zeros of the function are [MATH: x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\dots]

Content:
A general expression for the zeros is

Content:
[MATH: x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi.]

Content:
The Maxima of the Function

Content:
The function has a maximum when [MATH: x=0] and is periodic with period [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] that maximize cosine is

Content:
[MATH: x = 2n\pi.]

Content:
The Minima of the Function

Content:
The function has a minimum when [MATH: x=\pi] and is periodic with period [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] that minimize cosine is

Content:
[MATH: x = \pi + 2n\pi.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\cos{x}.]

Now, let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is true. The minimum value is [MATH: -1,] and the maximum value is [MATH: 1.] Therefore, the range is [MATH: [-1,1].]

  • Statement II is false. The function has a minimum at [MATH: x=\pi] and the period is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, the minimum values occur at [MATH: \pi+2n\pi.]

  • Statement III is true. These are the zeros of the cosine curve. The cosine curve has zeros at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2} + n\pi.]

In conclusion, only statements I and III are true.

items.title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cosine Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \cos x =- \dfrac {1}{3},] find the value of [MATH: 2\cos( x + 4\pi)+3.]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \cos x =- \dfrac {1}{3},] find the value of [MATH: 2\cos( x + 4\pi)+3.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y = \cos x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for any integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \cos{x} = \cos{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=2] into the right-hand-side of the above gives

[MATH: \cos x|= \cos (x + 2 ⋅ 2 ⋅ π); = \cos (x + 4π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \cos{x} =- \dfrac {1}{3},] then [MATH: \cos{(x+4\pi)} = - \dfrac {1}{3}.]

Finally, then

[MATH: 2\cos (x + 4π) + 3|= 2(− (1)/(3)) + 3; = − (2)/(3) + 3; = (7)/(3).]

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{4},] then find the value of [MATH: \cos (-x-6\pi).]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{4},] then find the value of [MATH: \cos (-x-6\pi).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\cos{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \cos{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]

  • Our graph is symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis. This means that [MATH: \cos{x}] is an even function, and we have [MATH: \cos(-x) = \cos{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \cos{x},] we have [MATH: \cos (− x − 6π)|= \cos (− x − 2π ⋅ 3); = \cos (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the evenness of [MATH: \cos{x},] we have [MATH: \cos (− x)|= \cos x; = (sqrt(3))/(4).]

Therefore, [MATH: \cos (-x-6\pi)= \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{4}.]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Cosine Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{4},] then find the value of [MATH: \cos (-x-6\pi).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:

[IMG: /graphics/dfab92fbee88df2003b54abc658b5d81]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \cos{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]
- Our graph is symmetric about the [MATH: y]-axis. This means that [MATH: \cos{x}] is an even function, and we have
[MATH: \cos(-x) = \cos{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \cos{x},] we have
[MATH: \cos (− x − 6π)|= \cos (− x − 2π ⋅ 3); = \cos (− x).]
- Secondly, using the evenness of [MATH: \cos{x},] we have
[MATH: \cos (− x)|= \cos x; = (sqrt(3))/(4).]

Therefore, [MATH: \cos (-x-6\pi)= \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{4}.]
